For either appliance, I’d choose the **[BLUETTI Elite 200 V2](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2)**. Its **2,600 W inverter** gives it headroom for a typical 1,800 W induction burner or kettle, and its **2,073.6 Wh battery** offers more cooking time than a smaller station. ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop))

A single induction burner can draw up to **1,800 W**. At full power, expect roughly **about an hour** from a 2,000 Wh-class station; lower heat settings and normal stop-and-start cooking can stretch that. ([PowerStationMatch](https://powerstationmatch.com/devices/induction-cooktop)) For a kettle, check its wattage label and make sure it’s below the station’s continuous output. One litre of water takes roughly **90–110 Wh** to boil, so battery capacity—not just wattage—determines how many boils you’ll get. ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-that-can-run-an-induction-cooktop))
